title: Supreme Court: 24-hour clock to produce detainees starts at detention, not formal arrest
dek: Anyone held beyond 24 hours from the moment their liberty is curtailed must be freed at once, the court ruled, overturning three High Court rulings and ordering magistrates to check.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Police and other investigating agencies must bring anyone they detain before a magistrate within 24 hours of the moment that person's liberty is first curtailed, not 24 hours from when the arrest is formally written down, the Supreme Court ruled on Thursday. Anyone held longer must be released at once.

The judgment, by Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar, settles a question on which High Courts had split, and closes what agencies had argued was a lawful "buffer zone" for questioning before a formal arrest. The court ordered that the ruling be sent to every state and Union Territory police chief, every High Court and every state judicial academy, so that it reaches police stations and magistrates' courts across the country.

## What the court decided

Article 22(2) of the Constitution says a person who is arrested and detained must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, leaving out only the time needed for the journey to the court. The question was when that clock starts.

The bench held that it starts "from the date and time of detention of the person detained when his liberty stands curtailed and not from the time of his formal arrest". No other period, such as time spent on searches, seizures or questioning, can be left out of the count. "Article 22(2) does not sanction exclusion of the time taken for enquiry and investigation before the arresting authority could effect arrest of the detainee," the judgment says.

The court went further than the 24-hour limit. Under Section 58 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which replaced Section 57 of the old Criminal Procedure Code, detention without a warrant must also not last longer than is reasonable in the circumstances. The judges said that applies even inside the 24 hours.

It laid down duties for magistrates:

- At the first production, a magistrate must record the actual date and time when the person's liberty was curtailed, and check whether the 24-hour deadline was met from that moment.
- If the deadline was breached, the person must be released immediately.
- Even if the person was produced within 24 hours, the magistrate must ask whether the detention was longer than reasonable, and may refuse to send the person to custody if it was.

The bench said three High Court rulings that had allowed the pre-arrest period to be left out of the count, by the Orissa High Court (Aryaman Pattnayak), the Madras High Court (Kannan) and the Kerala High Court (Arun K Thomas), "do not lay down the correct law". LiveLaw reported that the court approved a different Kerala High Court ruling, in Biswajith Mandal, which had held that the clock starts when liberty is effectively curtailed.

## The case

The appeal came from Tripura. According to the judgment, a team from the customs department's preventive force in Agartala intercepted a truck at 2 pm on 29 September 2025 and recovered 11.03 kg of methamphetamine tablets, known as yaba. The search continued at the customs office in Agartala and ended at 5 pm. The men were shown as formally arrested at 11 am and 11.15 am the next day, and were produced before a magistrate at 4.45 pm on 30 September, nearly 27 hours after they were stopped.

The agency argued that the men were merely intercepted at 2 pm, and that questioning under Section 67 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act created a period before arrest when Article 22(2) did not apply. The Tripura High Court refused bail on 29 April 2026, applying the strict bail conditions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act for large quantities of drugs.

The Supreme Court disagreed. From 2 pm on 29 September, it said, the men were under the control of the search team, so they should have been before a magistrate by 2 pm the next day. That made their detention after that point "illegal and unconstitutional". Separately, it noted that 18 hours passed between the end of the search at 5 pm and the formal arrest, with no explanation. "18 hours in custody without judicial oversight is a long period with misuse and abuse of authority a clear possibility," the judges wrote.

The court set aside the High Court's order and directed that the three appellants be produced before the Special Court within seven days and released on bail on conditions that court sets. It said that where Article 21, the right to life and liberty, is violated, the rigour of Section 37 of the NDPS Act "would have to give way", citing earlier rulings. The ruling does not decide whether the men are guilty; the drugs case against them continues.

## Why the court tied it to custodial violence

The judgment links the strict reading of the 24-hour rule to the long record of abuse in custody. "Custodial violence is an unfortunate reality of our country and is judicially acknowledged," it says.

It recalled the Bhagalpur blindings of prisoners in Bihar around 1980, which reached the Supreme Court in the Khatri cases, and the court's 1996 judgment in D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal, which set out rules for arrest after deaths in police custody. In D.K. Basu, the bench noted, the court had recorded that the worst violations take place when police avoid "recording the arrest" or describe the loss of liberty "merely as a prolonged interrogation". It also cited later orders requiring CCTV cameras in all police stations and in the offices of central agencies such as the CBI, NIA, Enforcement Directorate and Narcotics Control Bureau where people are questioned and held.

## What changes

For anyone stopped by police or a central agency, the ruling means the 24 hours begin when they are no longer free to leave, whether or not an arrest memo has been prepared. Agencies that routinely hold people overnight "for questioning" before showing a formal arrest the next morning now risk having the detention declared illegal at the first hearing.

The burden shifts to magistrates, who must now record the time of first detention in every case and check it against the 24-hour limit. Lawyers for the accused can be expected to raise the gap between interception and formal arrest in bail and remand hearings, particularly in cases under special laws such as the NDPS Act, where searches often take hours and bail is hard to get.

The judgment applies to all investigating agencies, including police, customs, and central bodies. The government and the agencies have not yet commented publicly on it.

## Key numbers

- 24 hours: the limit in Article 22(2) of the Constitution
- 2 pm, 29 September 2025: when the Tripura appellants were intercepted
- 4.45 pm, 30 September 2025: when they were produced before a magistrate
- 18 hours: unexplained gap between the end of the search and the formal arrest
- 3: High Court rulings the Supreme Court said were wrong in law
